metaTitle: Flying Ants: What They Are and Why They Swarm
metaDescription: Flying ants are winged males and young queens on a mating flight, not a species. When swarms happen, how long they last and what one in the house means.
h1: Flying Ants: Why They Swarm and What It Means in Your House
dek: Flying ants are ordinary ants at the one stage of life when some of them have wings. Here is what a swarm is, when and why it happens, how long it lasts, and how to read a swarm that turns up inside the house.
excerpt: Flying ants are the winged males and young queens of ordinary ant colonies. When they swarm, how long it lasts, and what a swarm inside the house tells you.

quickAnswer.lead: **Flying ants are not a separate species: they are the winged males and young queens that an established ant colony sends out to mate and start new colonies.** Outdoors, a swarm is normal and brief. Indoors it deserves a closer look, because [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ants_household_B6183.pdf) says winged ants swarming inside a home likely come from a colony located somewhere inside.
bullets: A carpenter ant colony usually does not produce winged ants until it is several years old and has about 2,000 to 3,000 workers, according to Penn State Extension.

Red imported fire ants usually fly at midday on a warm (above 74°F), sunny day following rain, in six to eight flights of up to 4,500 winged ants each between spring and fall, the University of Florida reports.

Swarming is short: the University of Wisconsin gives three to four days for citronella ants, and Utah State University says pavement ants can keep swarming inside a building for a few days to over a week.
Iowa State University's rule of thumb is that hundreds of winged ants indoors mean the colony is almost certainly in the house, while fewer than 10 were likely strays from an outdoor colony.
Winged carpenter ants are up to 3/4 inch long, and numerous ones at an indoor window probably came from a nest inside the house, Penn State says.

body.text: What are flying ants?

Flying ants are not a species of their own. They are the winged males and young queens, called swarmers or reproductives, that an established colony of ordinary ants produces so the species can mate and spread. [Iowa State University Extension's article on ant swarming](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/ant-swarming) describes swarmers as the queen and king ants that fly out to start a new colony, and points out that the worker ants people normally see are all females, while males just mate and die.

The flight is the first step in founding a colony. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's guide to household ant pests](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ants_household_B6183.pdf) explains that some species produce winged ants that swarm from the nest during certain times of the year, mate, and then form new colonies. A newly mated female becomes the queen. Once she finds a nesting site she loses her wings and begins to lay eggs, and she feeds the larvae herself until the first workers have developed. How the nest grows from there is covered in [the full reference on ants and how their colonies work](/learn/ants).

body.text: Do all ants swarm?

No. Texas A&M notes that in some ant colonies mating may occur within the nest without swarming, and that those ants form new colonies when one or more queens leave with some workers and brood for a new location. Its entry for pharaoh ants says their colonies include winged male and female reproductives, yet pharaoh ants do not swarm, and its table of common house-infesting ants gives them no swarming season. They multiply by budding, a process in which a large part of the colony moves to a new nesting site with some of its young. The same table says odorous house ants seldom swarm and that Argentine ant swarms are rare. For those small kitchen ants, a cloud of winged insects is the exception.
How do you know they are ants and not termites?

Check the wings, the antennae and the waist. Texas A&M's comparison chart says winged ants have two pairs of wings with the hind pair shorter, antennae that are usually elbowed, and a narrow waist between the thorax and abdomen. Winged termites have two pairs of wings of equal size and shape, hair-like antennae and no narrow waist. The side-by-side photos, the workers of each insect and the damage each one leaves are in [the comparison of flying ants and termites](/blog/flying-ants-vs-termites).

body.title: Rule out termites first
body.text: Iowa State says winged termites in a home are a strong indication that a termite colony may be eating the wood of the house. If the wings are all the same length and there is no narrow waist, have the insects identified before you assume they are ants.
Why do flying ants suddenly appear?

They appear suddenly because colonies release them together. Iowa State notes that a well-established ant colony may produce hundreds of swarmers, and that all the colonies of the same species in an area produce swarmers at the same time. That is why, at certain times of the year, the air can seem full of winged ants.

A colony has to mature before it can swarm. [Penn State Extension's carpenter ant fact sheet](https://extension.psu.edu/carpenter-ants) says a carpenter ant colony usually does not produce winged males and queens until it is several years old and has about 2,000 to 3,000 workers. Approximately 200 to 400 winged ants then develop in the summer, remain in the nest through the winter and leave the following spring or early summer. Fire ants get there sooner: [the University of Florida's profile of the red imported fire ant](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN352) says winged reproductives are produced after a colony reaches one year of age.

Weather picks the day. The University of Florida reports that fire ant mating flights usually occur at midday on a warm, sunny day following rain, with warm meaning above 74°F (24°C). Penn State says winged carpenter ants emerge from established colonies on warm days in the spring and early summer. These sources describe when flights happen. None of them explains why warmth and recent rain are the cue, so this page does not offer a reason.

The numbers explain why a swarm is hard to miss. The University of Florida describes six to eight fire ant mating flights, each of up to 4,500 winged ants, between spring and fall, and says that in the southern United States as many as 97,000 queens may be produced per acre of infested land per year. Which red ants are fire ants, and how their mounds and stings are handled, is covered in [the guide to red ants in the US](/blog/red-ants).
When is flying ant season?

There is no single flying ant season. Each species flies on its own schedule, mostly between spring and fall, and pavement ants can swarm in any month, winter included, where the nest sits near a heated slab. The table gathers the timing that university extension sources give, adding [Utah State University Extension's pavement ant fact sheet](https://extension.usu.edu/planthealth/research/pavement-ants) and [the University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension article on citronella ants](https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/citronella-ants/) to the publications cited above. The Texas A&M entries describe Texas and may not match other states.

body.text: How long do flying ants last?

Swarming lasts from a few days to over a week in the two species for which these extension sources give a figure. The University of Wisconsin says citronella ant swarming lasts only three to four days, and Utah State says winged pavement ants can continually swarm within a structure for a few days to over a week.

The individual ants do not stay flying ants for long either. Males die soon after mating, according to the University of Florida. A mated fire ant queen, its authors write, rakes her legs forward to snap her wings off at the base, then finds a spot to begin a colony, often under rocks or leaves or in a small crack or crevice. Within 24 hours of mating she will have laid 10 to 15 eggs. How long queens and workers survive after that is a separate question, answered in [the guide to how long ants live](/blog/how-long-do-ants-live).

What a swarm does not do is empty the nest. The swarmers leave an established colony behind them: Texas A&M describes a mature carpenter ant colony as holding winged males and females alongside sterile workers of various sizes and a wingless queen. When the winged ants are gone, the colony that produced them is still alive.

body.text: Flying ants in the house: what does an indoor swarm mean?

A swarm of flying ants inside the house usually means a colony is nesting in or under the building. Texas A&M states that when winged ants swarm in the home, it is likely that their colony is located somewhere inside. Iowa State adds two other possibilities: a colony near the foundation of the house, or a species that is attracted to lights at night.
How many flying ants are you seeing?

The count is the most useful clue. Iowa State's article says hundreds of swarmers indoors mean the colony is almost certainly in the house somewhere, in the walls, in rotten wood or under the slab. With fewer than 10, its advice is to keep an eye out for ant activity, because those were likely accidental invaders from an outdoor colony.

Where they gather tells you something as well. Penn State says that if numerous winged carpenter ants are found at windows inside the house, they probably came from an indoor nest. Utah State notes that in commercial buildings pavement ant swarmers work their way into occupied areas through walls and false ceilings, and that they are attracted to fluorescent lights, which draw them out of wall and ceiling voids and into rooms.

body.text: Why are there flying ants in the house in winter?

Flying ants indoors in winter point to a nest that the building itself is keeping warm. Penn State says carpenter ants hibernate, meaning they are inactive, during the winter, but will be active if a nest is located in a heated portion of a building. The same fact sheet says a colony's winged ants develop in summer and remain in the nest through the winter, so a nest in a heated wall already holds its swarmers during the cold months.

Pavement ants do something similar under concrete. Utah State says they swarm primarily in late spring but can swarm even in the winter if they are nesting near heated slabs. Citronella ants, also called larger yellow ants, are a third candidate at the cold ends of the season, though the source used here does not place them in midwinter. Wisconsin says they nest in moist soil along or under foundations and that their winged forms are most often seen in early spring (March and April) and again from late September to October. They give off a lemon or citronella odor when crushed, feed on aphid honeydew, have no interest in human food, and are described as a nuisance only when they swarm.
Are big flying ants in the house carpenter ants?

They may be, and size is the first check. Penn State describes winged carpenter ants as up to 3/4 inch long and workers as 1/4 to 1/2 inch, and Texas A&M also gives about 3/4 inch for the winged reproductives. Color is less reliable. Penn State calls the black carpenter ant a common invader of homes in the northeastern United States, but Texas A&M says that in Texas the same species, the largest of the state's carpenter ants, rarely causes a problem indoors, and that the workers of the species common indoors there have dull red bodies with black abdomens. [The guide to black ants around the home](/blog/black-ants) separates carpenter ants from the smaller dark species.

Winged carpenter ants indoors deserve a follow-up because of where the nest may be. Texas A&M says that if they are found in a home, it is likely that a colony is nesting indoors. Both sources are measured about the damage. Texas A&M says galleries can weaken structural timbers but calls tunneling into structural wood rare for the species that occur in Texas, and Penn State says the expansion of a nest into a building's wooden timbers rarely causes structural damage. Moisture is the thing to look for: Penn State says these ants seldom tunnel into dry, sound wood but may excavate moist, rotting wood, and it advises checking areas where wood may be wet or damp.

Finding one nest may not be the end of it. Penn State explains that an indoor nest may be a satellite of a parent colony outdoors, often in a tree, log or waste wood within 100 yards of the house, and that both have to be found and eliminated. The bite is the lesser problem, as the page on [whether carpenter ants bite](/blog/do-carpenter-ants-bite) explains. The nest is the real issue, and [how carpenter ant nests are tracked down](/blog/carpenter-ants-canada) has its own guide.
What should you do about flying ants in the house?

Remove the swarmers with a vacuum, confirm what they are, then deal with the nest that sent them. A spray aimed at the ants you can see is unlikely to settle it, because the colony stays where it is. Texas A&M's guide says insecticide sprayed on ant trails kills only a few foraging workers without eliminating colonies, and that indiscriminately spraying foraging ants or the area around the home will do little good.

items: **Make sure they are ants.** Look for elbowed antennae, a narrow waist and hind wings shorter than the front pair. If all four wings are the same length and there is no narrow waist, treat it as a possible termite swarm and have the insects identified.

**Vacuum them up.** Wisconsin calls vacuuming up the winged forms as they appear the easiest and most environmentally friendly way to control citronella ant swarmers, and a vacuum removes other indoor swarmers without a spray.

**Count them and note where they appeared.** Hundreds point to a colony in the building, and fewer than 10 point to strays, by Iowa State's rule of thumb. Texas A&M's advice for any ant problem is to note where most of the ants are appearing and whether they have wings, because the most important thing is to try to locate the nest.

**Get the species identified.** Iowa State calls identification the first step before any management, since it tells you whether the species forms colonies inside homes, where to look and what will work. Texas A&M suggests collecting ants with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol and putting them in an alcohol-filled vial for a county Extension agent to identify.

**Look for signs of the nest.** For carpenter ants, Texas A&M says to search for piles of sawdust-like wood scrapings and dead ant parts beneath exit holes. Penn State adds piles of coarse, stringy wood particles and a rustling sound in walls and ceilings.

**Fix moisture and close gaps.** Texas A&M's prevention list includes repairing dripping faucets and plumbing leaks, replacing wet or rotten wood, caulking cracks and crevices, and storing firewood away from the house. Penn State notes that carpenter ants usually will not infest sound wood with a moisture content below 15 percent.

**Treat the colony, not the swarm.** Texas A&M says an indoor nest that can be reached can be treated directly with an insecticide, and one that cannot be reached with baits. Choose a product labeled for that ant and for indoor use, and follow the label. Bait choice depends on the species: Wisconsin warns that citronella ants will not respond to normal ant baits.

body.text: If wingless workers are trailing indoors as well, [the step-by-step plan for ants in the house](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-house) covers following a trail back to its entry point, and the reasoning behind [baiting a colony instead of spraying the ants you can see](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-canada) is set out separately.
When should you call a professional?

Call one when a large swarm appears indoors and you cannot find the nest, or when the swarmers are carpenter ants. Texas A&M says reaching a colony sometimes means drilling holes into wood and wall voids, and that this is a job for a professional pest control operator who has the skill and equipment. Penn State is blunter about carpenter ants: it says a satellite colony inside a building is unlikely to be eliminated without materials applied by professional pest management companies. A suspected termite swarm is also a reason to call.
Are flying ants outside the house a problem?

Usually not. Texas A&M says winged ants swarming outside, such as around porch lights, should not be a concern, and that turning off porch lights or switching to yellow bug lights will discourage them. Iowa State draws the same line: most people are fine with winged ants outdoors and become more concerned when they find them inside the home. Where fire ants live, the swarm may end up in the pool. The University of Florida notes that winged fire ants are often attracted to swimming pools, where homeowners can find thousands of them trapped on the water's surface.

The exception is a species that is a problem in its own right. Texas A&M's table lists red imported fire ants as ants that both bite and sting and carpenter ants as ants that bite but do not sting, so the colony behind an outdoor swarm matters more than the swarm itself. [Which US ants bite, which sting and which do both](/blog/do-ants-bite) is covered in its own guide. An outdoor swarm can also seed an indoor nest: Texas A&M says newly mated females may choose indoor nesting sites if suitable ones are not available outdoors, which is a reason to fix wet wood and leaks and to caulk gaps before swarm season.

faqs.question: Do flying ants bite or sting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the species, because a flying ant is the winged form of an ordinary ant. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's table of house-infesting ants lists carpenter ants as ants that can bite but do not sting, and red imported fire ants as ants that both bite and sting. Those entries describe each species as a whole, and the sources used for this page do not say how readily the winged ants themselves bite or sting. The same publication says most people can tolerate fire ant stings, but some people are very sensitive to the venom and must seek medical attention. Anyone who has a strong reaction to a bite or sting should contact a healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Does one flying ant in the house mean an infestation?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Iowa State University Extension's rule of thumb is that fewer than 10 swarmers indoors were likely accidental invaders from an outdoor colony, and its advice is to keep an eye out for further ant activity. Hundreds indoors are a different matter: that many means the colony is almost certainly in the house, in the walls, in rotten wood or under the slab. The season counts as well. Winged ants indoors in winter suggest a nest in a heated part of the building, since Penn State Extension says carpenter ants are inactive in winter unless the nest is in a heated portion of a building.

faqs.question: Why do flying ants come out after rain?
faqs.answer: Extension sources confirm the pattern for some species, although the ones used for this page do not explain the reason. The University of Florida says red imported fire ant mating flights usually occur at midday on a warm, sunny day following rain, with warm meaning above 74 degrees Fahrenheit. Penn State Extension says winged carpenter ants emerge on warm days in spring and early summer. Iowa State University Extension adds that all the colonies of one species in an area produce their swarmers at the same time, which is why so many winged ants appear together.

faqs.question: Do flying ants lose their wings?
faqs.answer: The queens do. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension explains that a newly mated female loses her wings once she finds a nesting site and then begins laying eggs. The University of Florida describes how a red imported fire ant queen does it: she rakes her legs forward to snap her wings off at the base, then finds a spot to begin a colony, often under rocks or leaves or in a small crack. Within 24 hours of mating she will have laid 10 to 15 eggs. Males do not found colonies. They die soon after mating.

faqs.question: Can flying ants start a new nest inside my house?
faqs.answer: They can, but the first thing an indoor swarm tells you is that a nest may already be there. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension says newly mated females become the queens of new colonies and may choose indoor nesting sites if suitable ones are not available outdoors. The same publication says that when winged ants swarm in the home, their colony is likely located somewhere inside. Either way the response is the same: remove the swarmers, have the species identified, and fix the damp wood, leaks and gaps that make a house suitable for nesting.

faqs.question: Are flying ants attracted to light?
faqs.answer: Some are. Iowa State University Extension notes that some ant species are attracted to lights at night, which is one way a few swarmers from an outdoor colony end up indoors. Utah State University Extension says pavement ant swarmers are attracted to fluorescent lights, which draw them out of wall and ceiling voids and into rooms. For swarms around a porch, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension suggests turning off porch lights or switching to yellow bug lights to discourage them, and adds that winged ants swarming outside should not be a concern.
